passages.quote: Rapid localized corrosion may lead to penetration of the metal containing the coolant.
Ionization is the process of adding electrons to or removing electrons from atoms or molecules, creating ions.
Conductivity is a measure of the ability of a substance to allow electron flow.
Corrosion is the deterioration of a material due to interaction with its environment.
Electrolysis is the decomposition by electric current
This chapter will concentrate on the corrosion of metals in water-based environments (electrolytes).
Corrosion is electrochemical in nature because the corrosive chemical reactions involve transfer of charge.
The process in which electrons are given up and positive metal ions are formed is called oxidation.
In order for corrosion to occur, the micro-cells must also be connected through some conducting path external to the metal.
Oxidation is the process of losing electrons; reduction is the process of gaining electrons.
The metal atoms release electrons (are oxidized) and become positive ions. The site at which this occurs is known as the anode.
An oxidation process cannot take place without a simultaneous reduction (gain of electrons) process.
General corrosion is the process whereby the surface of a metal undergoes a slow, relatively uniform; removal of material.
Passivity is the characteristic of a metal exhibited when that metal does not become active in the corrosion reaction.
Passivity is caused by the buildup of a stable, tenacious layer of metal oxide on the surface of the metal.
In electrochemical cells, the decrease in cell potential caused by the operation of the cell (current flow) is called polarization.
Both concentration and activation polarization decrease the net oxidation-reduction reaction rate.

The two conditions typically required for a metal to undergo general corrosion are: 1) metal and water in the same environment, and 2) a chemical reaction between the metal and water that forms an oxide.
the oxide layer represents a barrier to continued corrosion and tends to slow the corrosion rate.
A rule of thumb is that the reaction rate doubles with a 20
Water velocities of 30 to 40 ft per second are usually considered to cause erosion.
The presence of oxygen in water to which iron is exposed increases the corrosion rate.
that remove the absorbed atomic hydrogen are called depolarizers.
Deposits, scale, or irregular surfaces create areas on the metal where local corrosion can initiate and proceed at a faster rate than normal.
This process, referred to as pretreatment, or pickling, involves careful control of reactor coolant water chemistry and temperature during the pretreatment period.
The use of cathodic protection, supplying an external electric current to the iron so that it acts as a cathode and has no anodic areas, is another method of preventative chemical control.
The three products formed from general corrosion of iron are FeO, Fe2O3, and Fe3O4.
Dissolved solids tend to make it easier for current to flow, which results in a higher corrosion rate.
corrosion products in the form of finely divided, insoluble oxide particles called crud become suspended in the reactor coolant or loosely adhere to metal surfaces.
The most undesirable characteristic of crud, however, is that it becomes activated when exposed to radiation.
The release of crud in this fashion is termed a crud burst.
Another corrosion byproduct is scale, which is made up of deposits on surfaces from the formation of insoluble compounds from normally soluble salts.
Galvanic corrosion is the corrosion that results when two dissimilar metals with different potentials are placed in electrical contact in an electrolyte.
The less resistant, active metal becomes the anodic corrosion site. The stronger, more noble metal is cathodic and protected.
Two locations susceptible to galvanic corrosion is a piping transition from one metal to another and a sacrificial anode (such as zinc).
The metal that corrodes to protect another metal is called a sacrificial anode.
Pitting corrosion occurs where the anodic site becomes fixed in a small area and the formation of holes (deep attack) in an otherwise unaffected area takes place.
Crevice corrosion is a type of pitting corrosion that occurs specifically within the low flow region of a crevice.
Pitting corrosion requires two conditions to occur, low flow and areas of both high and low oxygen concentration.
Pitting and crevice corrosion are a major hazard to a nuclear facility because of the rapid penetration of the metal with little overall loss of mass.
Stress corrosion cracking (SCC) is a type of intergranular attack corrosion that occurs at the grain boundaries under tensile stress.

Stress corrosion cracking occurs when three conditions are met; the alloy is susceptible to stress corrosion cracking, the alloy is exposed to specific environment, and the alloy is in a stressed condition.
According to the most widely accepted theory, stress corrosion cracking is caused by a process called chemisorption.
The formation of this chemisorbed layer greatly reduces the attraction between neighboring metal atoms.
SCC is of great concern because it can readily crack metal of appreciable thickness.
The three conditions that must be present for chloride stress corrosion to occur are as follows.
In stress cracking that is induced by a caustic environment, the presence of dissolved oxygen is not necessary for the cracking to occur.
Available data indicates that caustic concentrations greater than 10,000 ppm, and probably up to 50,000 ppm, are required to induce caustic stress cracking

summary.text: Corrosion is electrochemical in nature because the reactions involve a transfer of charge.
Passivity and polarization both slow or stop the corrosion process.
The three products formed from general corrosion of iron are FeO, Fe2O3, and Fe3O4.
Crud problems include fouling, radiation levels, hot spots, and waste disposal.
In galvanic corrosion, the active metal becomes anodic and the noble metal becomes cathodic.
Stress corrosion cracking can readily crack metal of appreciable thickness.

blend_notes.note: p.2 says the module concentrates on water-based environments. General electrochemistry, passivity, polarization, galvanic corrosion, and stress corrosion cracking are untagged. Pages built on water chemistry carry the Water-system only tag: general corrosion of iron, corrosion rate factors, chemical control, aluminum, crud, pitting, and chloride and caustic cracking.

The reactor coolant hydrogen discussion on p.16 is left off under the Nov 5, 2026 decision on water reactor coolant systems. Objective 1.14 and 1.15 on crud stay because they name reactor coolant generally, on a tagged page.

Table 1 on p.4 lists nickel at -2.250 volts, between cobalt at -0.277 and tin at -0.136, which looks like a misprint. It also shows iron with Fe+++ at -0.44, while the text uses Fe++. The table is not reproduced.

p.25 says a much larger surface area of the non-active metal accelerates attack, while p.26 says to choose areas so the protected material has a larger area than the active metal. The lesson lists only that surface areas are chosen, and no check tests the direction.
p.21 calls passivators a naturally active metal, while p.16 calls them chemical substances added to water. The lesson uses p.16. p.31 writes the ammonium ion as NH3+, and the lesson leaves it off.
p.20 says a pH between 4 and 10 gives a minimal corrosion rate, while p.15 says the rate is relatively independent of pH in that range for aerated water. The lesson uses p.15.
